name: Standing pose
blurb: Weight on one leg, hips and shoulders tilted: the base of every full-body pose
title: Standing Pose Reference: Contrapposto, Variations & Photo Tips
description: Standing pose reference for drawing and photos: contrapposto, weight shift, where the hands go, and how to stand so a full-body shot looks relaxed.
answer: A standing pose is any full-body pose where the figure supports itself on its feet. The ones that look natural almost always shift the weight onto one leg, so the hips tilt one way and the shoulders tilt the other, a balance known as contrapposto. Arms, head turn and foot placement then set the mood.

sections.h: Why a standing pose looks stiff or alive
body: Stand evenly on both feet with arms hanging and the body reads like a mannequin. Classical Greek sculptors solved this with contrapposto: one leg locked and carrying the load, the other bent and relaxed, so the pelvis drops on the relaxed side and the ribcage swings back to keep the head over the standing foot.

That small S-curve is why a character sheet turnaround can look neutral while a cover illustration feels like the character is about to speak. In Japanese fandom the plain full-body character portrait is called tachi-e (立ち絵), and even those usually carry a gentle weight shift.

sections.h: How to draw a standing pose

ol: Draw the line of action first: one gentle curve from head to the weight-bearing foot.
Find the balance line. A vertical dropped from the pit of the neck should land on or between the feet, usually over the standing foot.
Tilt the hip line and the shoulder line in opposite directions; the hip rises on the standing-leg side.
Foreshorten the feet. Seen at eye level they are ellipses resting on the ground plane, not flat side views.
Give the arms different jobs. Two arms hanging identically is the most common reason a figure looks stiff.

sections.h: How to pose and shoot a standing photo
body: Put the camera around the subject's waist or chest height for a true-to-life full body; dropping it to hip height and shooting slightly up lengthens the legs. A 50–85 mm lens on full frame keeps proportions natural, while a wide lens close up stretches whichever part is nearest.

ul: Shift the weight to the back foot and point the front toe toward the camera.
Give the hands something to do: a bag strap, a sleeve, a hair strand, a pocket.
Leave a small gap between arm and waist so the silhouette does not merge.
Turn the body about 30 degrees and bring the face back to the lens.

faq.a: It is the stance where one leg carries the weight and the other relaxes, so the hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions. It makes a standing figure look natural instead of rigid.

faq.q: Why do my standing figures look like they are falling over?
faq.a: The balance line is off. Check that a vertical line from the base of the neck lands on the weight-bearing foot or between both feet.

faq.q: What should I do with my hands in standing photos?
faq.a: Let them touch something, such as a pocket, strap, hair or the other arm, and keep them slightly apart from the body so they read clearly.
